lessons.title: Sliding Window Concept
lessons.concept: The sliding window technique maintains a contiguous range (window) over an array or string and moves it to satisfy a condition or compute an aggregate efficiently. Instead of recomputing from scratch for every window, it updates incrementally as the window expands or shrinks.
lessons.formula: Maintain window [left, right]. Expand right to include elements; shrink left when window violates condition or to optimize. Update answer during valid states.
lessons.worked_example: Max sum of subarray of size 3 in [2,1,5,1,3,2]: first window sum 8 (2,1,5), slide -> 7 (1,5,1), -> 9 (5,1,3), -> 6 (1,3,2). Max is 9.
mistakes: Recomputing window sum/state fully on every move instead of incremental update
Using sliding window on problems requiring non-contiguous elements
Off-by-one errors in window size or boundaries

lessons.title: Fixed-Size Window
lessons.concept: In a fixed-size window, the window length k stays constant. You compute the initial window result, then slide by removing the outgoing element and adding the incoming element to get the next window result in O(1) per step.
lessons.formula: window_sum = sum(arr[0..k-1]); for i>=k: window_sum += arr[i] - arr[i-k]; track max/min/condition.
lessons.worked_example: Average-like rolling sum for k=2 in [4,2,6]: windows [4,2]=6, [2,6]=8. Update by subtracting left element and adding right element.
mistakes: Forgetting to remove the element leaving the window
Starting sliding updates before the first full window is formed
Incorrect index for outgoing element (i-k errors)
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Variable-Size Window
lessons.concept: In a variable-size (dynamic) window, the window grows and shrinks to meet constraints, such as longest/shortest subarray with a property. Typically expand with right pointer and shrink with left pointer while condition is violated or to find optimal size.
lessons.formula: left=0; for right in range(n): add arr[right] to state; while state invalid: remove arr[left]; left++; update answer using current window [left,right].
lessons.worked_example: Longest subarray with sum <= 5 for [1,2,1,1]: expand to [1,2,1] sum 4 ok, add next 1 sum 5 ok (len 4), if next made invalid shrink from left.
mistakes: Shrinking with if instead of while when multiple removals may be needed
Updating answer at the wrong time (before window becomes valid)
Not maintaining auxiliary state (counts/sum) correctly on expand/shrink

questions.question: In a variable-size 'longest subarray where sum <= K' window, what happens when the running sum exceeds K?

options.B: The left edge advances (shrinks) until the sum is within K again
options.C: The right edge stops moving permanently

questions.explanation: Shrinking from the left restores the invariant sum(window) <= K while keeping the window as long as possible; the right edge continues expanding to probe longer candidates.

questions.question: Overall time complexity of a standard sliding window that moves left and right pointers at most n times each is:
questions.explanation: Each pointer advances monotonically at most n times, and per-move work is O(1) (with a counter/hashtable), so the total is O(n).

questions.question: Which condition is required for a correct sliding window update?

options.A: The array must contain distinct elements
options.B: Removing an element from the left must correctly decrement/undo its contribution to the window state
options.C: The window must always be odd-sized

questions.explanation: The window's aggregate (sum, count map, min/max structure) must be maintained exactly on both edges; forgetting to undo a left-edge contribution is the classic sliding-window bug.
